title: For more parents, ‘vaccine refusal’ is becoming vaccine delay, but it’s no less dangerous
content: Vaccine refusal doesn’t always sound like vaccine refusal in my pediatric office anymore. More and more parents are delaying vaccines and citing logistics, outsourcing the decision to the parent who isn’t in the room or simply wanting more time. I hear countless variations, but the result is often the same: Children leave my office unvaccinated. “Oh, we’re definitely not anti-vaccine. We’re just waiting for Dad.” Dad comes to the next visit. “I think Mom should be here when we do them.” “We are definitely going to vaccinate but we have a birthday party coming up, doctor; wouldn’t want her to be under the weather!” Another parent agrees to the vaccines, then slips out of the office before the nurse returns with them because the child is “beside himself.” Minutes earlier the kid was happily playing in the exam room. Vaccination has become so socially and politically loaded that some parents don’t want to identify with either camp. Rather than explicitly refusing, they postpone. This is a worrisome trend. During the 2025–2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners in the United States had completed the recommended measles, mumps and rubella series, down from 95.2% in 2019–2020. A few percentage points may not sound like much, but it meant 280,000 kindergartners attended school without documentation that they had completed the series. As of early October, the US had recorded 4,080 confirmed cases of measles in 2026 and two deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Compare that with 2,289 cases and three deaths in all of 2025, and only 285 cases and no deaths in 2024. For me, and many of my pediatric colleagues I speak to regularly, it has led to a realization: If the problem is no longer always explicit refusal, then our interventions can’t be solely designed around convincing self-declared vaccine skeptics. We have to get better at responding to “not today,” and many of us, understanding what is at stake, are working hard to do so. When a parent tells me they’ll vaccinate next time, I respect that choice, but I’m also clear with them about what waiting means: Their child is leaving my office without protection against a disease we can prevent. I also believe when a parent says, “Maybe next time,” their doctor’s office should offer a date and time. “We’ll do it later” is an intention, while “we’ll be back on Tuesday at 3:30 p.m.” is a plan. It’s a way to make it as easy as possible to return to get the child protected without calling the parent out. Lately, I also talk to parents a lot more about the diseases we are aiming to prevent than I had in the past. Vaccines have been so successful that many of today’s parents and many young pediatricians have never seen what these diseases can do. Most parents have never watched a baby struggle through pertussis or rotavirus or seen a child hospitalized with complications of measles. When the disease feels theoretical and every alleged vaccine side effect is just one social media search away, how parents calculate risk can become distorted. Recent measles outbreaks are a painful reminder that these diseases did not disappear; we stopped seeing many of them because vaccines worked. I am also discussing vaccines as a normal part of preventive care, which they are. Instead of asking what parents want to do about vaccines during their child’s visit, I have shifted to the same assumption we bring to the rest of preventive care: “Your child is due for these vaccines today.” We discuss the risks and benefits that are part of any recommendation we make, and parents can, and should, still ask questions. They still make the ultimate decision. But in a world filled with falsehoods and other noise, clear communication goes a long way. In nuanced conversations that are far from black and white, I have also found myself tailoring my approach and getting creative. If one parent tells me she needs the other before deciding, we call the other parent together. If both parents truly need more time, then I make sure they leave with reliable information and are part of the next conversation. I have also included grandparents and have even sat through social media videos and group chat posts to answer everyone’s questions. We need our health systems to make saying “yes” to vaccines as easy as possible. That means improving access, streamlining workflows, and allowing more time for counseling parents with questions and concerns. What I see in my exam room makes me wonder whether there may be an emerging group of parents who genuinely support vaccines while actively choosing to delay them. To better understand how to support these parents, researchers need to study that gap, and research requires funding. For pediatricians like me to do our jobs, we need to understand how people actually make decisions about vaccines and how those decisions are changing. At the end of the day, however, I don’t particularly care whether a parent calls themselves pro- or anti-vaccine. Viruses and bacteria don’t care either. What matters is the protection against measles, mumps, rubella, influenza, chicken pox and more — not the label. For every child to be protected, they need to get their shots, today.

A hormone that raises blood sugar may help put the brakes on a post-meal spike when fat reaches the gut before sugar. An international research team found that giving mice fat before glucose slowed stomach emptying and reduced the early blood sugar spike. The experiments suggest that the response involves cooperation between gut and pancreatic hormones and nerve signals, offering clues to why food order may matter. Human studies have already shown that eating vegetables, protein, or fat before carbohydrates can moderate post-meal blood sugar rises, an important treatment target in diabetes. Meal sequencing could therefore offer a practical dietary strategy that changes eating order without eliminating foods. “Our group has long been interested in practical dietary approaches that people can continue in everyday life,” says corresponding author Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University. “Meal sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups.” The stomach helps control how quickly nutrients reach the intestine. Slower emptying can spread out glucose delivery, tempering the early blood sugar rise. Researchers have also linked meal-sequencing benefits to increased release of incretin hormones, including GLP-1, which help lower blood glucose. Less clear was how these hormones interact with pancreatic hormones and nerve pathways. To investigate, the team fasted mice overnight and compared three feeding sequences: water followed by glucose, olive oil followed by glucose 15 minutes later, and glucose followed by olive oil 15 minutes later. They tracked blood glucose and plasma levels of insulin, glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. Blood measurements after oral acetaminophen provided an estimate of stomach-emptying speed. When olive oil came first, the mice showed a smaller early blood sugar rise and slower stomach emptying than when it came afterward. Giving fat first also increased early secretion of glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. These effects persisted in mice with type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency. Glucagon is best known for raising blood glucose, making its contribution here particularly intriguing. Blocking either glucagon or GLP-1 signaling alone did not weaken the glucose-lowering effect of giving olive oil first, but blocking both did, indicating that both pathways contribute to the response. The researchers also tested mice lacking the GLP-1 receptor and examined nerve involvement by tying off the vagus nerve below the diaphragm on both sides. The nerve experiments suggested that vagal pathways contribute to the response. Tests with other dietary fats helped establish that the findings were not unique to olive oil. “Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine,” says Yabe. Together with existing clinical evidence, the findings strengthen the case for testing practical meal-sequencing strategies in people with and without diabetes. The next challenge is to determine how reliably this hormone and nerve response translates into benefits during everyday meals. Reference: “Olive Oil Before Oral Glucose Delays Gastric Emptying and Lowers Glycemia Through Partially Redundant Glucagon and GLP-1 Signaling in Mice” by Yanyan Liu, Hiromi Tsuchida, Sodai Kubota, Saki Kubota-Okamoto, Takehiro Kato, Yukio Horikawa, Shin Tsunekawa, Hitoshi Kuwata, Yuuka Fujiwara, Yuji Yamazaki, Yuichiro Yamada, Hiroki Fujita, Katsumi Iizuka, Naoya Murao, Shinji Ueno, Yusuke Seino, Atsushi Suzuki, Yoshitaka Hayashi, Tsuyoshi Nakanishi, Daniel J. Researchers discovered that a diabetes medication altered how certain immune cells function, potentially reducing harmful inflammation. A medication already used to treat diabetes may protect the heart by changing how immune cells behave in the bloodstream. In a small human clinical trial, researchers found that the drug reduced inflammatory cell clusters associated with cardiovascular disease, with measurable effects appearing after just two weeks. The findings, published in the American Heart Association journal Circulation , provide the first direct evidence that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors can alter specific immune cells in humans. These medications are known for lowering blood sugar, promoting weight loss, and providing cardiovascular and kidney benefits, but their effects on inflammation have been less clear. Researchers at Vanderbilt Health studied 16 women with obesity and prediabetes who received the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin for three months. Blood samples collected before treatment, after two weeks, and after 12 weeks allowed investigators to track changes in immune activity. The team also examined a separate comparison group of women who followed a low-calorie diet for three months. Using advanced genetic sequencing and cellular imaging, the researchers identified a significant reduction in monocyte platelet aggregates (MPAs). These clusters form when blood-clotting cells (platelets) attach to immune cells (monocytes), creating structures associated with inflammation in blood vessels and cardiovascular disease. MPA levels declined significantly within two weeks of starting empagliflozin and fell further by the end of the study. The women in the diet comparison group did not show the same reduction, suggesting that the medication’s effects on these cells may extend beyond its influence on body weight. The researchers also identified evidence of “metabolic reprogramming” in monocytes (immune cells). These cells shifted away from a highly inflammatory state toward a more stable metabolic profile associated with normal cellular energy production. “There had been some suggestive studies in animals with these medications indicating they might be modulating the immune system — affecting inflammation — but that hadn’t really been shown in humans,” said Mona Mashayekhi, MD, PhD, Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Division of Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism at Vanderbilt Health. “This study provides the first direct evidence of SGLT2 inhibitors altering human immune cells, which may potentially reduce cardiovascular risk.” “This finding is significant because it’s the first time this medication has been shown to have an immune effect at the cellular level with some specificity. If we understand how these medicines are reducing obesity-associated inflammation and heart disease and kidney disease, then we can identify the best patient for this treatment or discover other drug targets in that pathway that could really be beneficial.” Mashayekhi and her colleagues have launched a randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Vanderbilt Health that aims to enroll 74 participants with obesity and metabolic syndrome. The study will examine immune changes over three months and analyze adipose tissue (fat) to investigate how the medication affects inflammation within the body. The larger trial will help determine whether the immune changes observed in the initial study can be confirmed under more rigorous conditions and clarify how SGLT2 inhibitors influence inflammation associated with metabolic disease. Reference: “SGLT2 Inhibitor Empagliflozin Reduces Circulating Monocyte-Platelet Aggregates: A Pilot Study” by B. Ilkin Safa, Jared M. Oakes, Joshua D. Simmons, Hui Nian, Leslie A. Kirk, Anna C.
